The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said it will not finalize methods for estimating emissions developed from a livestock study and plans to end a 2005 agreement with farms. EPA said monitoring data collected in 2005-2007 were too old and limited to support reliable methods because farm designs, production practices and technology have changed. EPA plans to notify participating operations and terminate the agreement; it said the decision does not change how it implements the Clean Air Act.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN warns climate adaptation funding leaves vulnerable countries exposed
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report says developing countries remain exposed to worsening floods, droughts and heat because adaptation funding is not reaching vulnerable communities at the scale required. Least-developed countries and small island states need an estimated $40 billion to $50 billion annually, equivalent to 3% to 4% of their gross domestic product, while support to least-developed countries fell 16% from 2022 to 2024. Adaptation measures include flood barriers, heat-resistant hospitals and drought-resilient water and farming systems. Low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides between 2020 and 2025. Communities also face obstacles to turning plans into projects, including weak institutional coordination and difficulty accessing funding for climate-related losses. At the COP31 climate conference, opening in Antalya on Nov. 9, campaigners are urging governments to set out a concrete funding plan and prioritize grants or concessional loans over high-interest borrowing for projects that generate little direct revenue. Concessional loans are easier to repay than high-interest loans.

items.title: [pbs.org] Greenland approves US defense pact, clearing path for expanded Arctic bases
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Greenland’s parliament voted 16-0 on Nov. 3, with seven lawmakers abstaining, to approve a security agreement with Denmark and the United States, clearing the way for expanded U.S. military access to the Arctic island. The pact permits two new U.S. defense sites and supports the Golden Dome missile-defense system while affirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. It would remain in force if Greenland later becomes independent. President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the agreement in September after Trump repeatedly pressed for U.S. control of Greenland and threatened force and tariffs against allies. Denmark has rejected a transfer of the territory but had been open to discussing a larger U.S. military presence. The Danish parliament is scheduled to take up the measure on Nov. 11 and vote on Nov. 19. The pact takes effect after the required Danish and Greenlandic parliamentary procedures and does not require U.S. Senate approval. Greenlandic officials and residents remain divided over whether the security arrangement brings tangible benefits to the island.

items.title: [globalnews.ca] U.S. Democrats take Congress as Canada keeps trade strategy unchanged
items.content_html:

Democrats won control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, but Canada says it will continue trade talks with President Donald Trump’s administration and pursue trade diversification. The new lawmakers take office in January. Canada’s Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the current Congress and administration remain in place and that Canada conducts trade talks with the U.S. executive branch. Prime Minister Mark Carney said talks had resumed after breaking down in August and that Washington had stepped back from some demands. U.S. tariffs target Canadian sectors including autos, steel, aluminum, forestry and manufactured goods. Ottawa has imposed counter-tariffs on about $27.6 billion in U.S. imports, while the trade dispute has disrupted exports and raised costs for manufacturers. The change in Congress does not itself end the tariffs. Analysts say the president retains executive authority over trade measures, and businesses warn uncertainty will persist until an agreement is reached. LeBlanc said he planned to speak with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in the coming days.

items.title: [Fast Company] Jack Dorsey’s Block is cutting jobs again. Here’s what makes these layoffs different
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Jack Dorsey’s fintech company, Block, began a second round of layoffs on Wednesday, months after cutting more than 4,000 jobs in February. The company has not said how many employees are affected at this time. 

The cuts hit the Customer Ops, Risk Ops, and Learning & Content Operations teams supporting Cash App, Block’s consumer financial services app, and Square, its tool for sellers. According to Business Insider, those teams will be “reducing the number of roles, changing some responsibilities, and shifting some reporting lines.” 

Affected employees are expected to receive a “separation package and transition support, similar to those affected in February 2026.” Block has not detailed the new terms. In February, laid-off employees received 20 weeks or more of severance pay, with the final amount dependent on tenure. Their packages also included equity vested until the end of May, six months of healthcare coverage, their company-issued work devices, and an extra $5,000.

Block did not respond to Fast Company’s request for comment as of publication. 

The layoffs came one day after Block reported its third-quarter results on Tuesday. The company said it raised its 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, up from its initial $12.51 billion estimate. It also projected a fourth-quarter gross profit of $3.32 billion. 

Block hasn’t explained what drove this round of layoffs. Earlier this year, Dorsey announced that the February layoffs were not because of financial issues, but because of “intelligence tools,” like AI.

“A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better,” Dorsey wrote on X then. “Intelligence tool capabilities are compounding faster every week.”

“We see an opportunity to move faster with smaller, highly talented teams using AI to automate more work,” Block CFO Amrita Ahuja said. 

Block is also continuing to build its own AI products. The company recently released Dessa, a speech-to-speech AI voice model trained on the recording of real human conversations.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Singapore Airlines said about 46,000 booking records may have been accessed in a breach at travel technology provider Amadeus, potentially exposing passenger names, booking references, itineraries and booking classes. About 620 records may also have included email addresses, phone numbers, travel-document details and KrisFlyer membership numbers. The airline said payment information was not exposed, bookings were not changed and its own systems were not breached. The unauthorized access involved booking data from August 2023 to September 2026. Cathay Pacific reported about 53,000 affected bookings, Japan Airlines about 92,000 affected customers and All Nippon Airways 37,800 affected records; Qantas is still checking whether its bookings were affected. Amadeus said it fixed the vulnerability and strengthened monitoring. Singapore Airlines is contacting customers with upcoming travel to change their booking references, while Singapore’s Personal Data Protection Commission said it is investigating.

items.title: [farmer.pl] Farmers urged to shred corn stalks to curb pests and disease
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

As Poland’s corn harvest continues, agronomic guidance recommends finely shredding stalks and other crop residues after harvest to reduce winter shelter for the European corn borer and limit disease in the next season. The borer’s larvae overwinter in stalks, while feeding damage can promote Fusarium infections that contaminate grain with mycotoxins. Residue management also affects soil organic matter: grain corn leaves substantial biomass in the field, while silage harvesting removes nearly all above-ground material. Guidance recommends accounting for soil moisture and the next crop; working wet soil can cause compaction, and fields vulnerable to erosion may need residue left on the surface.

items.title: [pbs.org] Clashes at Italian living-cost protests; 371 briefly detained
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Thousands of people demonstrated across Italy on Saturday, Oct. 24, against rising living costs and war. Police and protesters clashed in Rome, Turin and Bologna, while the Milan march was largely peaceful. Police used tear gas and water cannons in several cities. Authorities said nine people were arrested and 371 were temporarily detained in eight cities, including 110 minors. Demonstrators raised concerns about housing and fuel costs, wages, public services and military spending. Security measures followed the previous weekend’s looting and clashes in Milan, where shops in the fashion district boarded up windows as a precaution. items.title: [Macworld] Apple reportedly slashes employee AI usage limits amid ‘cost-cutting effort’
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Macworld

Apple took its time jumping on the AI bandwagon, announcing Apple Intelligence as late as 2024 (nearly three and a half years after the release of DALL-E, and one and a half after ChatGPT) then delaying some of the platform’s flagship features for years after that. But these days the company is a committed proponent of “truly helpful AI that’s centered around you and your needs,” as it writes on the dedicated Apple Intelligence page on its website.

Product pages for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo extol their ability to handle AI workloads, and similar language is used to market the iMac, iPad mini, Apple Watch Series 12, HomeView, and pretty much every other product Apple sells. Former CEO Tim Cook said AI is critical to Apple’s products back in 2023, while new boss John Ternus told Wired last month that the company is “absolutely going to leverage AI” to build incredible products.

However, as much as it encourages customers to enjoy the benefits of AI, Apple has seemingly soured on excessive use of the technology by its own employees. In a new report, Bloomberg claims the company has begun “reducing employee budgets for artificial intelligence usage as part of a cost-cutting effort.”

Citing anonymous people with knowledge of the change, leaker Mark Gurman says Apple last month reduced the daily AI spending cap for some engineers from $300 to $200, and is planning to make further cuts which could see limits drop as low as $100. “Many groups outside of engineering already face a $100 daily cap, but Apple has considered reducing that limit to as little as $25 for some teams,” Gurman adds. Staff who believe these limits will impede their ability to do their job can ask for an exemption.

The spending limits relate to the tokens used by AI providers to track the volume and nature of usage, and to set fees. Complex, data-intensive tasks such as debugging code may cost more tokens than the lighter usage typical among consumers.

Some Apple employees will therefore need to be more conservative in the data-processing demands they place on AI. But others, apparently, won’t need to change anything about their approach. Gurman’s sources claim that “few workers were using their full $300 daily allowances, making the previous limits unnecessarily generous,” which suggests the savings obtained through the measure will be small.

Aside from those public comments praising the usefulness of AI, this is a surprising stance from a company which in its most recent financial disclosure announced its “best fiscal year ever.” But Apple has long been a company obsessed with spotting and eliminating unnecessary costs, with Cook (who came from an operations background) famous for his ability to optimise a supply chain.

Last month’s initial AI spending cut, while it happened on Ternus’s watch, may have been a decision made, or at least floated, while Cook was still in charge. But the plan to cut deeper shows that Ternus is just as keen as his predecessor on running an efficient company.

And after all, as he said in the Wired interview linked above, “We don’t want to ship AI for AI’s sake. When we’re doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?”
